title: Your Students Want to Master What You’re Teaching Them
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that students, like teachers, are genuinely motivated by mastery because being good at things is enjoyable. The puzzle he poses is why, if mastery motivates, students are not eager for the mastery classrooms offer. His answer is that mastery is expensive: it costs time, sweat and frustration, and students often do not see that the payoff is worth the price. He uses difficult video games as a contrast case, noting that games pay for that cost through carefully scaffolded tutorials, staged progress and constant rewards. Rather than gamifying the classroom, which he doubts can generalize because marriage, work and citizenship will never be gamified, he proposes teaching students to approach life itself like a hard game through a "Do Hard Things" mindset. Along the way he applies the same logic to teachers, urging early-career teachers to pursue improvement rather than perfection so that the motivating effects of growing competence can kick in.
points: Stuart frames student motivation around the cost of mastery: students are not against knowledge, they simply do not see that the time, effort and frustration are worth paying.
Video games succeed at motivating hard work because they guide players through the costly path to mastery with tutorials, staged levels and frequent rewards.
He rejects gamification as the answer because the most important adult arenas, such as marriage, work, parenting and civic life, will keep requiring people to meet them on their terms.
The alternative he proposes is a "Do Hard Things" attitude in which students learn to set worthwhile challenges for themselves and treat life as an adventure of their own making.
Teachers are subject to the same dynamic, so early-career teachers who trade perfectionism for daily improvement find the work grows more motivating as competence grows.
quotes: Students want to be good at things because it is fun being good at things. In other words, they are motivated by being good at, or mastering, things.

This is why, if you're an early career teacher especially, you need to focus on improving, not on perfection. Once you're a few years into an aggressive “I'm going to get better today” mindset, this job starts being more motivating because you start being pretty good at it.
The problem with mastery is that it doesn't come cheap — it costs time, sweat, and frustration — and nobody likes buying something expensive that they supposedly “need” but don't desperately want.

Mastery's expense is why more of our kids aren't begging us to let them work on the difficult skills and subjects we teach. If there were a magic You Now Know All of World History pill, all of my students would take it. The problem with my students' motivation isn't that they're against gaining historical knowledge and skill; it's that many of them don't see that the mastery is worth the effort.

Why do kids pay the time/effort/frustration cost for video game mastery, then? Two reasons: 1) video games today are unmatched in their ability to guide players through the costly process of gaining mastery, and 2) they provide great incentives for being awesome at them.

Marriage, work, civic engagement, parenting — these are things that will probably just keep being the hardest, most worthwhile, most impactful things we do as humans. They will likely persist in requiring us to meet them on their terms, rather than them meeting us on ours. And so I don't see gamifying my world history class as a viable path for helping my students motivate themselves; rather, I think I need to show them that there is a way to live one's life kind of like a video game.

That is what “Do Hard Things” is about (see Fig. 1): setting worthwhile challenges for yourself and experimenting with realizing those challenges. When we adopt a “Do Hard Things” attitude, we step out of life's bleachers, walk into the arena, and find a throughline of adventure running through the stories we're creating.
